title: Mapping Climates and Moving Ranges
endLine: Climate gives a first guess; dispersal, neighbours and land shape ranges.

scenes.tts: Why does one hot region grow rainforest, another desert? And where will warming push species? Climate models turn thirty-year averages of warmth and rain into a testable first guess about where life occurs.
scenes.caption: Why does one hot region grow rainforest, another desert? And where will warming push species? Climate models turn 30-year averages of warmth and rain into a testable first guess about where life occurs.
scenes.visual: Split world (schematic): left shows a hot landscape dividing into lush rainforest and dry desert beside a rising mountain slope; right shows temperature and rainfall gauges averaging over 30 years into monthly bars that project a glowing boundary onto the left map.
scenes.narration: Why does one hot region grow rainforest, another desert? And where will warming push species? Climate models turn 30-year averages of warmth and rain into a testable first guess about where life occurs.

scenes.visual: Title card 'Mapping Climates and Moving Ranges' fades cleanly over the dimmed split world while clouds drift slowly across the landscape.

scenes.tts: A Walter-Lieth diagram plots monthly temperature beside rain. A month reads dry when rain in millimetres falls below twice its temperature in degrees Celsius. The factor two is an empirical plant-stress marker, not a water balance. Köppen-Geiger rules sort climates in steps: aridity, then temperature class, then subtype rules.

The factor two is an empirical plant-stress marker, not a water balance. Köppen-Geiger rules sort climates in steps: aridity, then temperature class, then subtype rules.
scenes.visual: Right panel draws a Walter-Lieth climate diagram (schematic) with 10 °C aligned to 20 mm; where the blue rain curve dips under the red temperature curve, dry months shade amber, with the label 'dry: rain < 2 × temperature'. Below, a three-step Köppen-Geiger ladder highlights 'Arid?', 'Temperature class', and 'Subtype rules', tinting matching climate zones on the left map.

The factor two is an empirical plant-stress marker, not a water balance. Köppen-Geiger rules sort climates in steps: aridity, then temperature class, then subtype rules.

scenes.tts: Species distribution models link one species to climate. Following Hutchinson in 1957, climate variables become axes of niche space. A niche is the conditions where a population replaces itself without immigrants. The models fit the climates where the species was recorded.
scenes.caption: Species distribution models link one species to climate. Following Hutchinson in 1957, climate variables become axes of niche space. A niche is the conditions where a population replaces itself without immigrants. The models fit the climates where the species was recorded.
scenes.visual: Right panel morphs from the climate diagram into a two-axis niche space (schematic) with temperature and rainfall axes; occurrence dots on the left map fly across to plot a shaded envelope in niche space, which projects back onto the left landscape as a band labelled 'Occupied climate'.
scenes.narration: Species distribution models link one species to climate. Following Hutchinson in 1957, climate variables become axes of niche space. A niche is the conditions where a population replaces itself without immigrants. The models fit the climates where the species was recorded.

scenes.tts: As climate warms, an isotherm, a line of equal temperature, climbs uphill. Its speed equals warming divided by cooling per hundred metres. Say a slope warms zero point three degrees Celsius a decade and cools zero point six degrees per hundred metres. How far uphill each decade?
scenes.caption: As climate warms, an isotherm, a line of equal temperature, climbs uphill. Its speed equals warming divided by cooling per 100 metres. Say a slope warms 0.3 °C a decade and cools 0.6 °C per 100 metres. How far uphill each decade?
scenes.visual: Left mountain slope (schematic example) highlights a glowing blue isotherm contour partway up; right panel shows the formula 'isotherm climb = warming ÷ cooling per 100 m', with '0.3 °C / decade' and '0.6 °C / 100 m' appearing as spoken. Question banner appears: 'How far uphill each decade?'
scenes.narration: As climate warms, an isotherm, a line of equal temperature, climbs uphill. Its speed equals warming divided by cooling per 100 metres. Say a slope warms 0.3 °C a decade and cools 0.6 °C per 100 metres. How far uphill each decade?

scenes.visual: The question banner, formula, and inputs stay on screen while the blue isotherm contour pulses gently along the mountain slope without climbing yet.

scenes.tts: Zero point three divided by zero point six is zero point five. Times one hundred metres, the isotherm climbs fifty metres each decade. The measured median uphill shift is eleven metres a decade. Eleven over fifty is twenty-two percent, so such a species falls behind.
scenes.caption: 0.3 divided by 0.6 is 0.5. Times 100 metres, the isotherm climbs 50 metres each decade. The measured median uphill shift is 11 metres a decade. 11 over 50 is 22%, so such a species falls behind.
scenes.visual: Computed math steps animate on the right as spoken: '0.3 ÷ 0.6 = 0.5', then '0.5 × 100 m = 50 m / decade' as the blue isotherm climbs 50 m up the left slope. A green species band shifts only 11 m uphill, opening an amber lag bracket labelled '11 / 50 = 22%'.
scenes.narration: 0.3 divided by 0.6 is 0.5. Times 100 metres, the isotherm climbs 50 metres each decade. The measured median uphill shift is 11 metres a decade. 11 over 50 is 22%, so such a species falls behind.

scenes.tts: A range map blurs three things: tolerable conditions, neighbours, and places reached. Immigrants can sustain a sink population where local deaths beat births. Unreached suitable places look empty. So models map occupied conditions, not the fundamental niche, where a species could persist without competitors or enemies. Transplants inside, at and beyond the edge test this. If only beyond-range plantings fail, conditions there are implicated.

scenes.visual: Left map (schematic) highlights two mismatches in place: arrows of incoming seeds sustain a pulsing 'Sink' patch outside the niche band, while an unreached 'Empty suitable' patch stays blank. Right niche space dims the outer 'Fundamental niche' outline to the smaller occupied zone; transplant pins drop inside, at and beyond the range edge, and only the beyond-range pins fade ('If only beyond fails: conditions').

scenes.tts: Open weather stations miss forest shade. In 2019, De Frenne and colleagues found understories averaged about four point one degrees Celsius cooler in maximum temperature. Fire, soils and forest loss also reshape vegetation and ranges. Good models report confidence and keep projections apart from observations.
scenes.caption: Open weather stations miss forest shade. In 2019, De Frenne and colleagues found understories averaged about 4.1 °C cooler in maximum temperature. Fire, soils and forest loss also reshape vegetation and ranges. Good models report confidence and keep projections apart from observations.
scenes.visual: Left forest slope compares an open-ground weather station thermometer against a shaded understory logger showing '−4.1 °C in maximum temperature, on average' (De Frenne et al. 2019), then flashes schematic icons of fire and cleared lower forest. Right panel adds cell confidence shading and separates two labelled tracks: 'Observed' vs 'Scenario projection'.
scenes.narration: Open weather stations miss forest shade. In 2019, De Frenne and colleagues found understories averaged about 4.1 °C cooler in maximum temperature. Fire, soils and forest loss also reshape vegetation and ranges. Good models report confidence and keep projections apart from observations.

scenes.tts: In 2018 and 2023, Hylke Beck and colleagues mapped Köppen-Geiger climates at about one kilometre, with confidence levels. About five percent of non-Antarctic land changed major class between 1901 to 1930 and 1991 to 2020. By 2071 to 2099, scenarios project five to thirteen percent. A class change is not yet a biome change.
scenes.caption: In 2018 and 2023, Hylke Beck and colleagues mapped Köppen-Geiger climates at about 1 kilometre, with confidence levels. About 5% of non-Antarctic land changed major class between 1901 to 1930 and 1991 to 2020. By 2071 to 2099, scenarios project 5% to 13%. A class change is not yet a biome change.
scenes.visual: Left continent map sharpens into a fine 1-km Köppen-Geiger grid (schematic) with confidence shading (Beck et al. 2018, 2023). Right bar chart from the study's values: 'Observed: ~5%' (1901–1930 to 1991–2020) beside 'Projected (2071–2099): 5% low to 13% high emissions'; a small note reads 'class change ≠ biome change'.

scenes.tts: In 2011, Chen, Thomas and colleagues pooled land range shifts. Median shifts were sixteen point nine kilometres poleward and eleven metres uphill per decade, largest where warming was greatest. In 2014, Hargreaves, Samis and Eckert reviewed one hundred eleven transplant tests beyond range edges. Only forty-six percent placed the edge at a niche limit. Others pointed to dispersal limits or sinks.
scenes.caption: In 2011, Chen, Thomas and colleagues pooled land range shifts. Median shifts were 16.9 kilometres poleward and 11 metres uphill per decade, largest where warming was greatest. In 2014, Hargreaves, Samis and Eckert reviewed 111 transplant tests beyond range edges. Only 46% placed the edge at a niche limit. Others pointed to dispersal limits or sinks.
scenes.visual: Left map and slope show poleward ('16.9 km / decade') and uphill ('11.0 m / decade') median arrows, longer where warming was greater (Chen et al. 2011). Right panel (Hargreaves, Samis & Eckert 2014, 111 tests) shows three separate bars, '46% niche limit', '26% dispersal limit', '23% sink', with the note 'shares do not add to 100%', then dims into the end card.
scenes.narration: In 2011, Chen, Thomas and colleagues pooled land range shifts. Median shifts were 16.9 kilometres poleward and 11 metres uphill per decade, largest where warming was greatest. In 2014, Hargreaves, Samis and Eckert reviewed 111 transplant tests beyond range edges. Only 46% placed the edge at a niche limit. Others pointed to dispersal limits or sinks.
